issues.description: Class attribute/constructor mismatch for Animal: The problem statement UML (Animal class) declares two attributes (name: String and age: int) and a constructor Animal(String, int). The solution repository's Animal.java declares only a single field 'name' and a constructor Animal(String). The template Main.java uses single-argument subclass constructors (e.g., Seal("Clarabelle")), matching the solution but conflicting with the UML. This discrepancy leaves students unsure whether to implement an 'age' field and a two-parameter constructor or to follow the template/tests and implement only a single-argument constructor and name field.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the specification and code consistent. Either: (A) Update the problem statement UML to remove the 'age: int' attribute and the two-argument Animal(String,int) constructor so Animal only requires a name (and update UML lines accordingly), or (B) update the template and solution to add an 'age' field to Animal, change Animal constructor to Animal(String, int), add corresponding getters/setters, update all subclass constructors to accept and forward an age parameter, and update example usages in Main to pass an age.

issues.description: Constructor parameter mismatch for Animal and subclasses: The UML in the problem statement specifies a constructor Animal(String, int) (a two-parameter constructor), but the solution's Animal.java defines Animal(String) and subclass constructors (e.g., Seal) in the solution and the template's example usage use single-argument constructors like Seal("Clarabelle"). This inconsistent constructor signature across artifacts leaves students uncertain which constructor signature to implement and will cause compilation or test failures if they follow the UML but the tests expect single-argument constructors (or vice versa).
issues.suggestedFix: Align constructor signatures across all artifacts. Either: (A) Change the UML/problem text to require Animal(String) (single-argument) and update the UML constructor line to Animal(String) so it matches the template/example and solution; or (B) change the template and solution so Animal and all subclasses use Animal(String, int) (add age field, adjust subclass constructors and example usages in Main to pass both name and age). Update tests and examples accordingly so all artifacts use the same constructor signature.

issues.description: Concept: the Animal class API (attributes and constructor). Problem statement (UML) declares Animal with two attributes: name: String and age: int, and a constructor Animal(String, int). Template and solution use a different API: the Solution's Animal class defines a single-argument constructor Animal(String) and no age attribute, and the example usage in the Template Main constructs Seal, Pig, Goat with a single String argument. This mismatch means a student reading the UML/description may implement Animal(String,int) and an age field (or expect subclasses to require age), while the provided code and reference solution use only Animal(String). This inconsistency hinders mapping the requirement to the code and can block or confuse students about which constructor and attributes to implement.
issues.suggestedFix: Reconcile the Animal API across all artifacts. Two consistent options: (A) Simplify UML/problem statement to match code: remove the age attribute and the two-argument constructor from the UML and textual description so Animal has only name and a single-argument constructor Animal(String); update any UML constructor signature to Animal(String). Or (B) Extend template and solution to match UML: add private int age to Animal, implement a two-argument constructor public Animal(String name, int age), and update all subclasses (Seal, Pig, Goat) to provide matching two-argument constructors and forward age to super; update example usages in Main and tests to pass an age. Choose one option and apply it to problem_statement.md, template files (src/...), and the solution so all three artifacts use the same Animal API.
